body.text: The fates of Wile E. Coyote and his raison d’être, potential prey and nemesis, the Road Runner, have been entwined since 1949, when they made their debut as Looney Tunes cartoon characters. Coyote, with his lean and hungry look, single-mindedly pursued the impossible: the Road Runner, forever unattainable, always just out of reach, who zips heedlessly past him with a cheery “meep-meep.” Coyote constructs elaborate traps, complex contraptions that inevitably fail, their parts almost always supplied by the Acme company.

These two characters are at the centre of David Green’s entertaining feature Coyote vs Acme. But as the title implies, it’s the relationship between user and supplier that provides the impetus for the movie. Coyote isn’t just fighting fate and gravity: he’s up against the extreme end of corporate capitalism.

There are echoes of the highly successful Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988) in this live-action-plus-cartoon combo. It is a deft amalgam of capers, stunts, sight gags and comic performances, and a suitably topical exposé of monumental malfeasance. Coyote vs Acme, written by Samy Burch, neatly incorporates the animation dynamic into a larger story.

The company, we learn, might have started out small, as a mere cartoon anvil manufacturer, but it has become the world’s largest corporation. One of its corporate ads proclaims, “We’re a company of family values that values its family… of companies.” Yet for some reason the products Coyote keeps using, from magnet gloves to rocket skates, are as flimsy and unreliable as ever.

Coyote’s lightbulb moment (in this instance a neon sign) comes when he sees a TV commercial spruiking a legal firm that specialises in cartoon-related small claims. He hotfoots it to Albuquerque, New Mexico, to hire lawyer Kevin Avery (Will Forte), Harvard grad turned ambulance chaser. Avery’s technique is to settle: a few hundred dollars for each client. But Coyote, as always, has bigger plans. He’s determined to sue the company for every defective product he’s used. He has an ally, Avery’s niece Paige (Lana Condor), who is interning with the firm. And so the fight begins, as the team uncovers a mysterious Project Sisyphus that is the key to Coyote’s problems.

Coyote, mercifully, isn’t given a voice: instead, he communicates using signs (one of which reads “It’s a limited number of signs”). He can be infuriating, but his relentless, never-say-die attitude starts to have an effect on Avery. Will Forte does a nice job of conveying the character’s gradual shift from hangdog capitulation to righteous indignation; John Cena, as Avery’s old law-school nemesis, Acme corporate lawyer Buddy Crane, is equally effective in contrasting fashion; there’s something intriguingly cartoonish about his delivery and physicality.

In the world of Coyote vs Acme, the existence of cartoon characters is more or less taken for granted. They are simply there — or, in Acme’s view, there to be exploited. Looney Tunes stalwarts such as Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Tweetie Pie and Foghorn Leghorn have supporting roles. Dr Lorre (a Looney Tunes figure inspired by actor Peter Lorre) is another key figure in the narrative. Voice actor Eric Bauza supplies the voices for most of them.

Coexistence extends to objects. In one scene, Judge Troppogrosso (Luis Guzmán), who hears Coyote’s case, has both an actual gavel and a cartoon gavel at his disposal. Crane wields an anguished cartoon pencil that he aggressively snaps, making a drawer full of seemingly sentient pencils shiver apprehensively in anticipation.

The inspiration provided by Ian Frazier’s 1990 New Yorker piece, also titled “Coyote vs Acme,” is acknowledged in the credits, and there is a scene in which Coyote briefly leafs through a copy of the magazine. The name of the law firm, Avery, Jones and Maltese is a shoutout to Tex Avery, Chuck Jones and Michael Maltese, famed Looney Tunes directors; the latter two were the creators of Coyote and the Road Runner.

The film is framed by two contrasting acknowledgements of its own fraught post-production history. The first one is a footnote to the Warner corporate logo, stating that the company is “a wholly owned subsidiary of the Acme corporation.”

The story of how the movie almost got buried in the Warner vaults is comically in tune with Coyote vs Acme’s narrative. In 2023 Green delivered a completed film that performed well for test audiences. But Warner Bros decided not to release it, and declined for some time to consider offers from distributors interested in taking it on. The plan was to shelve it and take what has been estimated to be a $30 million write-down, something they did with two other projects. There was, however, a public and industry backlash, and the company finally relented, selling the movie to an indie distributor.

Having had a near-death experience at the hands of Warner Bros, the movie miraculously, like Coyote, survived to fight another day. At the end of the credits comes a dedication “to everyone who posted, shared, held up signs, and spoke out when it counted. This film made it to the big screen because of you.”

Watching Alexandre Koberidze’s Dry Leaf, it helps to surrender. It’s not difficult to do — there’s something disarming and absorbing about the paths the film takes, its asides and impulses, its look, sound and aura, the thoughts it sets in motion.

The opening images hint at what is to come. They are simple, evocative. Shadows of trees on the side of a building. Two dogs asleep on the pavement. A cat blinking. Several shots from different angles of the bronze statue of a footballer. A leaf on the ground, a billowing white curtain. Beyond the images themselves, something about the look of the film is evident and intriguing.

Georgian director Koberidze shot his first feature, Let the Summer Never Come Again (2017) on a 2008 Sony Ericsson mobile phone, and he uses it once again for Dry Leaf, his third film. Its low resolution might seem like a limitation to struggle with, for filmmaker and viewer alike. Images can be soft and hazy, definition is lost, borders blur, pools of darkness gather, images pixelate, and there’s a kind of unsteadiness even in stillness. But before long the constraints start to look like gifts. Even in a work that runs just over three hours, they remain a pleasure.

There is a story underpinning the film, a journey to follow. Irakli (played by David Koberidze, the director’s father), who lectures in sport at a university, learns that his daughter, Lisa, has taken off. In the letter to her parents he reads aloud, she says that she wants to disappear for a while, that she needs to do this, and that they should not worry.

Lisa is a photographer for a sports magazine, and her most recent, unfinished project involved travelling around the countryside researching locations for a story on football fields in small villages around Georgia. Irakli decides to leave the city and go on a similar road trip with Levan (Otar Nijaradze), the journalist colleague who had accompanied her on the location reconnoitre. Somehow, this feels to him like a way of finding her, or at least getting closer to her.

Levan is Irakli’s companion the entire way: he is there, in the passenger seat or alongside him, at every step. Yet although we hear Levan’s voice, we never see him; as a voiceover explains, “Levan, like many others in this film’s reality, is invisible.” This might sound ridiculous, but it is surprisingly easy to accept. There are more people in the film we can’t see, although other characters evidently do. It is one of many small moments of uncanniness, unexplained yet resonant, that punctuate the film.

And so the road trip begins, a haphazard journey with objectives, obstacles and small surprises. Landscapes have a kind of flowing, abstract quality; colours can seem luminous, objects shimmer, take on a talismanic quality, shapes in the distance change from one thing to another. Figures seem to disappear into the landscape and then return as we watch. Night footage is a source of constant, somehow satisfying bewilderment; a zoom in and out feels like alchemy.

It is also evident from the very outset that sound is as important as image. Alexandre’s brother, Giorgi Koberidze, composed the remarkable score, a work that perfectly illuminates and expands the world of Dry Leaf. There’s an incisive aspect to it, it can feel like the piano accompaniment to a silent movie, it is by turns percussive, playful, exalting, surprising. Giorgi Koberidze came on the shoot; he is also the film’s sound recordist and sound designer, and ambient sound and effects are part of the architecture of the score.

The images and sounds might have magical or inventive aspects, but encounters with strangers — even the invisible ones — have a solid, grounded quality. As Irakli and Levan make their way from one small rural community to another, some things feel consistent. When Irakli shows Lisa’s picture to people, they are quick to say that they’ve never seen her. When he asks the way to the nearest football field, he’s almost invariably told, “Just follow the road,” and that’s more or less what happens. Occasionally these encounters are brief; sometimes they unfold more gradually. Animals are significant presences; dogs, cats, sheep, horses, cattle, the occasional donkey. Sometimes they are figures in the distance; sometimes they provide encounters that carry as much weight as any human contact.

And always there’s the search for the next football field. There’s a simplicity to their shape and structure, to the essence of the goal — three lines, two posts and a crossbar. The fields are mostly empty, sometimes seemingly abandoned. Occasionally Irakli and Levan come across children playing football, or simply kicking a ball around, and there’s a sense that the game exists beyond the spaces in which it is played. When a boy says that the football ground is being repurposed, Irakli asks him where he plays. “Everywhere,” the boy replies. It’s an answer that speaks to the film as a whole.

The title itself has football significance. “Dry leaf” is a term coined to describe the dead-ball free kick perfected in the 1950s by the Brazilian player Didi, in which the ball dropped suddenly and unpredictably, impossible for the goalkeeper to anticipate, and something of an enigma to the person who kicked it. It feels like the perfect name for a film that is about the inevitable and the random, about circles, lines and mysteries, and the contemplation of a leaf on the ground. •
Coyote vs Acme and Dry Leaf are on limited release from 17 September.
